newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Armenia has mixed reaction to Azeri pipeline idea.
newsitem.headline: Armenia has mixed reaction to Azeri pipeline idea.

text.p: Armenia said on Friday it was interested in the idea of building a pipeline across its territory to carry Azeri oil to Western markets, but ruled out the idea of swapping territory for it.

An Armenian presidential spokesman was responding to a suggestion by Azeri President Haydar Aliyev on Thursday that a pipeline might be built in exchange for Armenia surrendering territory captured in fighting over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.
"By all means, building a pipeline through the Armenian territory is profitable for all," Armenian spokesman Levon Zurabyan told Reuters. "Armenia is interested in it."
"But at the same time, we do not see any relation between the pipeline's route and the settlement of the Karabakh conflict."
Separatist Armenian forces still hold 20 percent of Azerbaijan's territory, including the disputed enclave, captured during the fighting in the early 1990s.

Aliyev had previously rejected the idea a pipeline could be built across Armenia in return for the Armenians giving up the disputed territory. But when asked about it on Thursday at a briefing for foreign journalists in Baku, he said: "Such a variant could be considered."
Azerbaijan depends on pipelines through Russia for shipping oil from its huge deposits to world markets and is keen to find alternative routes. Armenia would earn big transit fees for any pipeline.
If a pipeline were to be built, it would probably be funded by a 13-member international consortium led by British Petroleum PLC and Norway's Statoil Den norske state oljeselskap AS (Statoil).
The consortium signed an $8 billion deal with the Azeri government in 1994 to develop three offshore fields, and the first crude oil from the project is due to come on stream later this year.

The consortium, the Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), plans to use two existing pipelines to get early oil to Black Sea outlets, but the pipelines do not have the capacity to handle later peak production from the project.
AIOC, which is considering various options, says it will announce later this year where it will build a new pipeline needed to accommodate full production.
Karabakh was incorporated into Azerbaijan in the 1920s despite having a predominantly Armenian population.

A 1994 ceasefire ended the territorial dispute, which began when Nagorno-Karabakh broke away in the late 1980s. But a political settlement to the conflict, which has killed thousands of people, is still a long way off.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright expressed concern on Thursday at the lack of progress in settling the conflict and urged the parties to stick to the truce, Itar-Tass news agency said.
